title: Complex numbers II: exponential form, De Moivre, roots

problems.html: Write each number in exponential form r eiθr\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}reiθ with r>0r>0r>0 and −π<θ≤π-\pi<\theta\le\pi−π<θ≤π: (a) 1+i,(b) −3,(c) 2i,(d) −1−i,(e) 3−i,(f) −2+23 i.\text{(a) } 1+\mathrm{i},\quad\allowbreak \text{(b) } -3,\quad\allowbreak \text{(c) } 2\mathrm{i},\quad\allowbreak \text{(d) } -1-\mathrm{i},\quad\allowbreak \text{(e) } \sqrt3-\mathrm{i},\quad\allowbreak \text{(f) } -2+2\sqrt3\,\mathrm{i}.(a) 1+i,(b) −3,(c) 2i,(d) −1−i,(e) 3​−i,(f) −2+23​i.
hints: Exponential form needs exactly the two numbers polar form needed: the modulus rrr and an argument θ\thetaθ, since reiθ=r(cos⁡θ+isin⁡θ)r\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}=r(\cos\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin\theta)reiθ=r(cosθ+isinθ).
Sketch each point before reaching for an arctangent — it is the quadrant, not the ratio b/ab/ab/a, that decides the argument.
The window −π<θ≤π-\pi<\theta\le\pi−π<θ≤π then settles the rest: a third-quadrant point takes a negative argument, and the negative real axis takes π\piπ rather than −π-\pi−π.
problems.format: the six arguments in order; π as pi

problems.html: Write each in Cartesian form a+iba+\mathrm{i}ba+ib: (a) 2 eiπ/3,(b) 3 eiπ,(c) 2 e−iπ/4,(d) 4 ei3π/2,(e) ei5π/6.\text{(a) } 2\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\pi/3},\quad\allowbreak \text{(b) } 3\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\pi},\quad\allowbreak \text{(c) } \sqrt2\,\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}\pi/4},\quad\allowbreak \text{(d) } 4\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}3\pi/2},\quad\allowbreak \text{(e) } \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}5\pi/6}.(a) 2eiπ/3,(b) 3eiπ,(c) 2​e−iπ/4,(d) 4ei3π/2,(e) ei5π/6.
hints: This is the easy direction: reiθ=rcos⁡θ+i rsin⁡θr\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}=r\cos\theta+\mathrm{i}\,r\sin\thetareiθ=rcosθ+irsinθ, so it is two evaluations and a multiplication.
Two of these sit squarely on an axis, where one of the cosine and sine vanishes and there is nothing left to compute.
In (d) the angle 3π2\tfrac{3\pi}{2}23π​ lies outside the principal window; that is harmless, since cosine and sine do not care which turn you are on.
problems.format: (b), (c), (d) in Cartesian form

problems.html: Evaluate eiπ/2\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\pi/2}eiπ/2, ei2π\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}2\pi}ei2π, e−iπ\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}\pi}e−iπ and eiπ/3\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\pi/3}eiπ/3, and state Euler’s identity.
hints: Each of these is a point on the unit circle at the stated angle — read off its cosine and its sine.
ei2π\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}2\pi}ei2π is a full turn and e−iπ\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}\pi}e−iπ is a half turn, so both land somewhere you already know without any computation.
Euler's identity is simply θ=π\theta=\piθ=π substituted into eiθ=cos⁡θ+isin⁡θ\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}=\cos\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin\thetaeiθ=cosθ+isinθ, rearranged so that one side is zero.
problems.format: the first three values, comma-separated

problems.html: Let z=2 eiπ/6z=2\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\pi/6}z=2eiπ/6. Write down eiπ/2z\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\pi/2}zeiπ/2z in exponential form, and describe geometrically the effect of multiplying a complex number by (i) i\mathrm{i}i, (ii) eiπ\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\pi}eiπ, (iii) e−iπ/2\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}\pi/2}e−iπ/2.
hints: ∣eiα∣=1|\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\alpha}|=1∣eiα∣=1, so multiplying by it cannot change a modulus. Only the argument can move.
Multiplying by eiα\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\alpha}eiα adds α\alphaα to the argument, which is an anticlockwise turn through α\alphaα about the origin.

So write each of i\mathrm{i}i, eiπ\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\pi}eiπ and e−iπ/2\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}\pi/2}e−iπ/2 as eiα\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\alpha}eiα and name the turn — a negative α\alphaα is a clockwise one.
problems.format: modulus and argument of the product; π as pi

problems.html: Use De Moivre’s theorem to simplify (cos⁡θ+isin⁡θ)4(\cos\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin\theta)^{4}(cosθ+isinθ)4 and (cos⁡θ+isin⁡θ)−2(\cos\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin\theta)^{-2}(cosθ+isinθ)−2.
hints: cos⁡θ+isin⁡θ\cos\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin\thetacosθ+isinθ is just eiθ\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}eiθ, so raising it to a power only multiplies the angle.

De Moivre says (cos⁡θ+isin⁡θ)n=cos⁡nθ+isin⁡nθ(\cos\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin\theta)^{n}=\cos n\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin n\theta(cosθ+isinθ)n=cosnθ+isinnθ, and it holds for every integer nnn, negative ones included.
For n=−2n=-2n=−2 that gives cos⁡(−2θ)+isin⁡(−2θ)\cos(-2\theta)+\mathrm{i}\sin(-2\theta)cos(−2θ)+isin(−2θ); now use that cosine is even and sine is odd to tidy the signs.
problems.format: the n in cos nθ + i sin nθ for each

problems.html: Compute, using the exponential form: (a) (1+i)4,(b) (3+i)3,(c) (1−i)6,(d) (2 eiπ/5)10.\text{(a) } (1+\mathrm{i})^{4},\quad\allowbreak \text{(b) } (\sqrt3+\mathrm{i})^{3},\quad\allowbreak \text{(c) } (1-\mathrm{i})^{6},\quad\allowbreak \text{(d) } \bigl(2\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\pi/5}\bigr)^{10}.(a) (1+i)4,(b) (3​+i)3,(c) (1−i)6,(d) (2eiπ/5)10.
hints: Convert to exponential form first. A power then costs one power of the modulus and one multiplication of the angle.
For (a), 1+i=2 eiπ/41+\mathrm{i}=\sqrt2\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\pi/4}1+i=2​eiπ/4, so the fourth power has modulus (2)4(\sqrt2)^4(2​)4 and argument 4⋅π44\cdot\tfrac{\pi}{4}4⋅4π​.
Reduce the resulting angle by multiples of 2π2\pi2π before converting back — in (c) you land on −3π2-\tfrac{3\pi}{2}−23π​, which points the same way as π2\tfrac{\pi}{2}2π​.
problems.format: (a)–(d), comma-separated

problems.html: Find all the (a) square roots of i\mathrm{i}i, and (b) fourth roots of 111.
hints: Write the number in exponential form, then remember that its argument is only fixed up to 2π2\pi2π — that is exactly where the extra roots come from.
For an nnnth root, take the real nnnth root of the modulus and divide θ+2πk\theta+2\pi kθ+2πk by nnn, for k=0,1,…,n−1k=0,1,\dots,n-1k=0,1,…,n−1.
In (b), 1=ei01=\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}0}1=ei0, so the four arguments are 2πk4\tfrac{2\pi k}{4}42πk​ — a quarter turn apart, starting from 111 itself.
problems.format: the fourth roots of 1, from 1, anticlockwise

problems.html: Plot the four fourth roots of unity 1,i,−1,−i1,\mathrm{i},-1,-\mathrm{i}1,i,−1,−i on an Argand diagram, mark the unit circle, and name the regular polygon they form.
hints: All four numbers have modulus 111, so they lie on the unit circle; only their arguments differ.
Those arguments are 0,π2,π,3π20,\tfrac{\pi}{2},\pi,\tfrac{3\pi}{2}0,2π​,π,23π​ — equally spaced, as the nnnth roots of unity always are.
Four points equally spaced around a circle are the vertices of a regular quadrilateral. Name it.
problems.format: the name of the polygon

problems.html: State, with the fundamental theorem of algebra in mind, how many roots in C\mathbb{C}C (counted with multiplicity) each has: (a) a degree-555 polynomial; (b) z7−3=0z^{7}-3=0z7−3=0; (c) (z−1)2(z2+1)=0(z-1)^{2}(z^{2}+1)=0(z−1)2(z2+1)=0. True or false: every real cubic has at least one real root?
hints: The fundamental theorem says a polynomial of degree nnn has exactly nnn roots in C\mathbb{C}C, provided each is counted with its multiplicity.
So the only work is finding the degree. In (c) do not solve anything — just add up the degrees of the factors, remembering that (z−1)2(z-1)^2(z−1)2 contributes two.
For the true/false part: a real cubic has three roots, and non-real ones come in conjugate pairs. A pair uses up two of the three, so what is forced about the remaining one?
problems.format: (a), (b), (c), then true or false

problems.html: By expanding (cos⁡θ+isin⁡θ)2(\cos\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin\theta)^{2}(cosθ+isinθ)2, derive the identities for cos⁡2θ\cos 2\thetacos2θ and sin⁡2θ\sin 2\thetasin2θ.
hints: Expand (cos⁡θ+isin⁡θ)2(\cos\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin\theta)^2(cosθ+isinθ)2 as an ordinary bracket, keeping the real and imaginary parts apart as you go.
De Moivre says that same expression equals cos⁡2θ+isin⁡2θ\cos2\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin2\thetacos2θ+isin2θ.
Two complex numbers agree exactly when their real parts and their imaginary parts separately agree — so a single expansion delivers both identities at once.
problems.format: cos 2θ and sin 2θ at θ = π/6, to 3 d.p.

problems.html: Using cos⁡θ=12(eiθ+e−iθ)\cos\theta=\tfrac12(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}+\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}\theta})cosθ=21​(eiθ+e−iθ), evaluate cos⁡(i)\cos(\mathrm{i})cos(i) in terms of e\mathrm{e}e. (The general identity cos⁡(ix)=cosh⁡x\cos(\mathrm{i}x)=\cosh xcos(ix)=coshx is built up in the tutorial.)
hints: Do not try to picture this one; simply substitute θ=i\theta=\mathrm{i}θ=i into the formula you are given.
The exponents become i⋅i=−1\mathrm{i}\cdot\mathrm{i}=-1i⋅i=−1 and −i⋅i=1-\mathrm{i}\cdot\mathrm{i}=1−i⋅i=1, so both exponentials turn into ordinary real numbers.
You are left with 12(e−1+e)\tfrac12(\mathrm{e}^{-1}+\mathrm{e})21​(e−1+e), which is a hyperbolic function evaluated at 111.
problems.format: the value of cos(i), to 4 d.p.

problems.html: (a) Write 5cos⁡(ωt+π3)5\cos(\omega t+\tfrac{\pi}{3})5cos(ωt+3π​) and 2sin⁡ωt2\sin\omega t2sinωt as phasors P=A eiφP=A\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\varphi}P=Aeiφ. (b) The phasor 3 e−iπ/23\,\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}\pi/2}3e−iπ/2 represents which real signal Acos⁡(ωt+φ)A\cos(\omega t+\varphi)Acos(ωt+φ)?
hints: A phasor records only the amplitude and the phase of a cosine, discarding the eiωt\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\omega t}eiωt that every term in the problem shares.
Everything must be written as a cosine first: sin⁡ωt=cos⁡(ωt−π2)\sin\omega t=\cos(\omega t-\tfrac{\pi}{2})sinωt=cos(ωt−2π​), so a sine term picks up a phase of −π2-\tfrac{\pi}{2}−2π​.
For (b) read the process backwards — the modulus is the amplitude and the argument is the phase sitting inside the cosine.
problems.format: amplitude and phase of each in (a); π as pi

problems.html: Let z=3+iz=\sqrt3+\mathrm{i}z=3​+i and w=1+iw=1+\mathrm{i}w=1+i. Write zzz and www in exponential form, then find zwzwzw and z/wz/wz/w in both exponential and Cartesian form.
hints: Convert both numbers to exponential form first; the index laws then do all of the work.
z=2 eiπ/6z=2\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\pi/6}z=2eiπ/6 and w=2 eiπ/4w=\sqrt2\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\pi/4}w=2​eiπ/4. Multiply moduli and add arguments, or divide and subtract.

For the Cartesian forms it is faster to expand (3+i)(1+i)(\sqrt3+\mathrm{i})(1+\mathrm{i})(3​+i)(1+i) directly and to use the conjugate trick on the quotient — the point of the exercise is that the two routes must agree.
problems.format: the arguments of zw and z/w; π as pi

problems.html: (a) Rotate z=3+4iz=3+4\mathrm{i}z=3+4i anticlockwise by π2\tfrac{\pi}{2}2π​ about the origin, and then (separately) clockwise by π2\tfrac{\pi}{2}2π​. (b) Rotate 2+2i2+2\mathrm{i}2+2i anticlockwise by π4\tfrac{\pi}{4}4π​. Give exact Cartesian answers.
hints: Anticlockwise by π2\tfrac{\pi}{2}2π​ is multiplication by eiπ/2=i\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\pi/2}=\mathrm{i}eiπ/2=i; clockwise by the same angle is multiplication by −i-\mathrm{i}−i.
So (a) is two one-line multiplications, with no trigonometry involved at all.
In (b) the point already has argument π4\tfrac{\pi}{4}4π​, so adding another π4\tfrac{\pi}{4}4π​ lands it on the imaginary axis — exponential form makes that immediate.
problems.format: the two rotations of z in (a)

problems.html: Prove by induction that (cos⁡θ+isin⁡θ)n=cos⁡nθ+isin⁡nθ(\cos\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin\theta)^{n}=\cos n\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin n\theta(cosθ+isinθ)n=cosnθ+isinnθ for all integers n≥1n\ge1n≥1. (Pure-maths.)
hints: Induction on nnn: verify the case n=1n=1n=1, then assume the statement at n=kn=kn=k and derive it at n=k+1n=k+1n=k+1.

The inductive step starts (cos⁡θ+isin⁡θ)k+1=(cos⁡kθ+isin⁡kθ)(cos⁡θ+isin⁡θ)(\cos\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin\theta)^{k+1}=(\cos k\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin k\theta)(\cos\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin\theta)(cosθ+isinθ)k+1=(coskθ+isinkθ)(cosθ+isinθ), using the hypothesis on the first factor.
Both factors have modulus 111, so the polar product rule — multiply moduli, add arguments — finishes it without a single trigonometric expansion.
problems.format: the value of (cos θ + i sin θ)⁶ at θ = π/6

problems.html: Compute (1+i)8(1+\mathrm{i})^{8}(1+i)8 and (3+i)6(\sqrt3+\mathrm{i})^{6}(3​+i)6 using De Moivre’s theorem.
hints: Convert, raise, convert back. The binomial theorem would need nine terms for the first of these; De Moivre needs one line.
1+i=2 eiπ/41+\mathrm{i}=\sqrt2\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\pi/4}1+i=2​eiπ/4, so the eighth power has modulus (2)8(\sqrt2)^{8}(2​)8 and argument 8⋅π4=2π8\cdot\tfrac{\pi}{4}=2\pi8⋅4π​=2π.
An argument of 2π2\pi2π is a full turn, so that answer is a positive real number. In the second the argument comes out as exactly π\piπ, which puts it on the negative real axis.
problems.format: (1+i)⁸ and (√3+i)⁶, comma-separated

problems.html: Evaluate (−1+i)10(-1+\mathrm{i})^{10}(−1+i)10, and confirm your answer by squaring −1+i-1+\mathrm{i}−1+i first.
hints: Put −1+i-1+\mathrm{i}−1+i into exponential form. It is in the second quadrant, so its argument is 3π4\tfrac{3\pi}{4}43π​ and not −π4-\tfrac{\pi}{4}−4π​.
The tenth power then has modulus (2)10(\sqrt2)^{10}(2​)10 and argument 30π4=15π2\tfrac{30\pi}{4}=\tfrac{15\pi}{2}430π​=215π​; subtract multiples of 2π2\pi2π until that is manageable.
For the check, square −1+i-1+\mathrm{i}−1+i first and raise the result to the fifth power — far less arithmetic than expanding the tenth power directly.
problems.format: the value, in Cartesian form

problems.html: Find (a) the cube roots of 888 and (b) the fourth roots of −16-16−16. In each case give exact Cartesian values and describe the polygon they form on the Argand diagram.
hints: Write the right-hand side in exponential form, then apply the root formula: the real nnnth root of the modulus, and arguments (θ+2πk)/n(\theta+2\pi k)/n(θ+2πk)/n.
In (a) the modulus is 81/3=28^{1/3}=281/3=2 and θ=0\theta=0θ=0, so the arguments are 0,2π3,4π30,\tfrac{2\pi}{3},\tfrac{4\pi}{3}0,32π​,34π​.

In (b) start from −16=16 eiπ-16=16\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\pi}−16=16eiπ — that non-zero starting angle is exactly what tilts the square. Note that all nnn roots share a single modulus, which is why they always sit on one circle.
problems.format: the modulus of the roots in (a), then in (b)

problems.html: Find all sixth roots of unity in Cartesian form, and verify that they sum to zero. Why does this generalise to all n≥2n\ge2n≥2?
hints: The nnnth roots of unity are ei2πk/n\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}2\pi k/n}ei2πk/n for k=0,…,n−1k=0,\dots,n-1k=0,…,n−1; here that means six points a sixth of a turn apart.
For the sum, pair each root with its conjugate — the imaginary parts then cancel two at a time.

For the general case, the roots form a geometric series with ratio ω=ei2π/n\omega=\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}2\pi/n}ω=ei2π/n. Sum it with the standard formula and use ωn=1\omega^{n}=1ωn=1 together with ω≠1\omega\ne1ω=1.
problems.format: the sum of the six roots

problems.html: Solve z3=−27iz^{3}=-27\mathrm{i}z3=−27i, giving the three roots in exponential and Cartesian form.
hints: Put the right-hand side into exponential form first: −27i-27\mathrm{i}−27i has modulus 272727 and sits on the negative imaginary axis.
So the modulus of each root is 271/3=327^{1/3}=3271/3=3, and the arguments are −π/2+2πk3\dfrac{-\pi/2+2\pi k}{3}3−π/2+2πk​ for k=0,1,2k=0,1,2k=0,1,2.
Work the three values of kkk through in order. One of them gives a purely imaginary root, which is a useful check that you have the arithmetic right.
problems.format: the arguments for k = 0, 1, 2; π as pi

problems.html: Using De Moivre and the binomial theorem, show that cos⁡3θ=4cos⁡3θ−3cos⁡θ\cos 3\theta=4\cos^{3}\theta-3\cos\thetacos3θ=4cos3θ−3cosθ and sin⁡3θ=3sin⁡θ−4sin⁡3θ\sin 3\theta=3\sin\theta-4\sin^{3}\thetasin3θ=3sinθ−4sin3θ.
hints: Expand (cos⁡θ+isin⁡θ)3(\cos\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin\theta)^{3}(cosθ+isinθ)3 with the binomial theorem, tracking the powers of i\mathrm{i}i carefully.
By De Moivre that expansion also equals cos⁡3θ+isin⁡3θ\cos3\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin3\thetacos3θ+isin3θ, so match real parts against real and imaginary against imaginary.
The real part still contains sin⁡2θ\sin^{2}\thetasin2θ; replace it with 1−cos⁡2θ1-\cos^{2}\theta1−cos2θ, and do the corresponding substitution in the imaginary part, to reach the stated forms.
problems.format: the coefficients in cos 3θ, then in sin 3θ

problems.html: Use the inverse Euler formula to write sin⁡4θ\sin^{4}\thetasin4θ as a sum of cosines of multiples of θ\thetaθ.
hints: The inverse Euler formula sin⁡θ=eiθ−e−iθ2i\sin\theta=\dfrac{\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}-\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}\theta}}{2\mathrm{i}}sinθ=2ieiθ−e−iθ​ turns a power of a sine into a binomial expansion.
Raising it to the fourth power gives a front factor of 1(2i)4=116\dfrac{1}{(2\mathrm{i})^{4}}=\dfrac{1}{16}(2i)41​=161​, since i4=1\mathrm{i}^{4}=1i4=1.

Expand with the coefficients 1,−4,6,−4,11,-4,6,-4,11,−4,6,−4,1, then pair each eikθ\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}k\theta}eikθ with its partner e−ikθ\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}k\theta}e−ikθ to recover 2cos⁡kθ2\cos k\theta2coskθ.
problems.format: the constant, cos2θ and cos4θ coefficients

problems.html: (a) Show cos⁡(ix)=cosh⁡x\cos(\mathrm{i}x)=\cosh xcos(ix)=coshx and sin⁡(ix)=isinh⁡x\sin(\mathrm{i}x)=\mathrm{i}\sinh xsin(ix)=isinhx. (b) Hence evaluate cos⁡(iln⁡2)\cos(\mathrm{i}\ln 2)cos(iln2) exactly.
hints: Use the inverse Euler formulas and substitute θ=ix\theta=\mathrm{i}xθ=ix; the imaginary unit in the exponent then cancels against the one in the argument.
For the sine you will need 1i=−i\dfrac{1}{\mathrm{i}}=-\mathrm{i}i1​=−i to tidy up the factor in front.
For (b), cosh⁡(ln⁡2)=12(eln⁡2+e−ln⁡2)\cosh(\ln 2)=\tfrac12\left(\mathrm{e}^{\ln 2}+\mathrm{e}^{-\ln 2}\right)cosh(ln2)=21​(eln2+e−ln2), and both exponentials collapse to ordinary numbers.
problems.format: the value of cos(i·ln2), as a fraction

problems.html: (a) Combine 3cos⁡ωt+4sin⁡ωt3\cos\omega t+4\sin\omega t3cosωt+4sinωt into a single sinusoid Rcos⁡(ωt−α)R\cos(\omega t-\alpha)Rcos(ωt−α). (b) Combine 2cos⁡ωt+2cos⁡(ωt+π2)2\cos\omega t+2\cos(\omega t+\tfrac{\pi}{2})2cosωt+2cos(ωt+2π​) likewise.
hints: Turn every term into a cosine, take its phasor, add the phasors as complex numbers, and read the answer off the sum.
sin⁡ωt=cos⁡(ωt−π2)\sin\omega t=\cos(\omega t-\tfrac{\pi}{2})sinωt=cos(ωt−2π​), so a sine term contributes a phasor with argument −π2-\tfrac{\pi}{2}−2π​ — that is, a negative multiple of i\mathrm{i}i.
The modulus of the resulting phasor is the amplitude RRR and its argument gives the phase. Notice that the amplitude is not the sum of the two original amplitudes.
problems.format: R and α in (a); α to 3 d.p.

problems.html: (a) To exponential form (−π<θ≤π-\pi<\theta\le\pi−π<θ≤π): −4-4−4,   3i\;3\mathrm{i}3i,   −2−2i\;-2-2\mathrm{i}−2−2i,   −1+3 i\;-1+\sqrt3\,\mathrm{i}−1+3​i. (b) To Cartesian form: 5 eiπ/25\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\pi/2}5eiπ/2,   2 e−i2π/3\;2\,\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}2\pi/3}2e−i2π/3,   2 ei3π/4\;\sqrt2\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}3\pi/4}2​ei3π/4.
hints: Both directions rest on the same two facts: r=∣z∣r=|z|r=∣z∣ with the argument fixed by the quadrant, and reiθ=rcos⁡θ+i rsin⁡θr\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}=r\cos\theta+\mathrm{i}\,r\sin\thetareiθ=rcosθ+irsinθ.
Sketch each point in (a) before committing to an argument; the required window is −π<θ≤π-\pi<\theta\le\pi−π<θ≤π.
In (b) every angle is a standard one, so the cosines and sines can be written down without a calculator.
problems.format: the four arguments in (a); π as pi

problems.html: Simplify to a single r eiθr\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}reiθ (then to Cartesian if clean): (a) eiπ/3⋅eiπ/6\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\pi/3}\cdot\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\pi/6}eiπ/3⋅eiπ/6, (b) 8 ei5π/62 eiπ/3\dfrac{8\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}5\pi/6}}{2\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\pi/3}}2eiπ/38ei5π/6​, (c) (2 eiπ/8)4\bigl(\sqrt2\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\pi/8}\bigr)^{4}(2​eiπ/8)4.
hints: Exponential form exists precisely so that these become index laws: add exponents to multiply, subtract to divide, multiply to take a power.
The moduli are handled separately by ordinary arithmetic — 8/28/28/2 in (b), and (2)4(\sqrt2)^{4}(2​)4 in (c).
All three answers end up on the imaginary axis, so each has argument π2\tfrac{\pi}{2}2π​ once the angle is reduced.
problems.format: (a), (b), (c) in Cartesian form

problems.html: A square is centred at the origin with one vertex at z0=2+iz_{0}=2+\mathrm{i}z0​=2+i. Find its other three vertices by repeatedly multiplying by i\mathrm{i}i, and state the side length.
hints: The vertices of a square centred at the origin are a quarter turn apart, and a quarter turn is multiplication by i\mathrm{i}i.
So apply i\mathrm{i}i to z0z_0z0​ repeatedly; each step is one line of arithmetic and no trigonometry.
The side length is the distance between two adjacent vertices, so take the modulus of their difference — it is not the circumradius ∣z0∣|z_0|∣z0​∣.
problems.format: the other three vertices, in order

problems.html: Let α∈R\alpha\in\mathbb{R}α∈R. Show that for all z,w∈Cz,w\in\mathbb{C}z,w∈C, ∣eiαz∣=∣z∣\left|\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\alpha}z\right|=\left|z\right|​eiαz​=∣z∣ and ∣eiαz−eiαw∣=∣z−w∣\left|\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\alpha}z-\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\alpha}w\right|=\left|z-w\right|​eiαz−eiαw​=∣z−w∣. What does the second identity say geometrically?
hints: Everything follows from the single fact ∣eiα∣=1|\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\alpha}|=1∣eiα∣=1, together with ∣zw∣=∣z∣ ∣w∣|zw|=|z|\,|w|∣zw∣=∣z∣∣w∣.
For the second identity, factor eiα\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\alpha}eiα out of the difference before taking any modulus.
Preserving every distance is exactly what it means for a map of the plane to be rigid. Say which rigid motion this one is.
problems.format: the value of |e^{iα}|

problems.html: Evaluate (a) (1−i3)9(1-\mathrm{i}\sqrt3)^{9}(1−i3​)9, (b) (2+2i)5(2+2\mathrm{i})^{5}(2+2i)5, (c) (1+i3+i)12\left(\dfrac{1+\mathrm{i}}{\sqrt3+\mathrm{i}}\right)^{12}(3​+i1+i​)12.
hints: The same recipe each time: exponential form, then one power, then back.
In (b) the modulus is 22=23/22\sqrt2=2^{3/2}22​=23/2, so the fifth power has modulus 215/22^{15/2}215/2 — keep it as a power of 222 rather than reaching for a decimal.
In (c) simplify the quotient inside the bracket first. It collapses to a single r eiθr\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}reiθ with a small angle, and only then should you raise it to the twelfth power.
problems.format: (a), (b), (c), comma-separated

problems.html: Assuming De Moivre for positive integers, prove it for negative integers n=−mn=-mn=−m (m∈Nm\in\mathbb{N}m∈N). [Hint: (cos⁡θ+isin⁡θ)−1=cos⁡θ−isin⁡θ(\cos\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin\theta)^{-1}=\cos\theta-\mathrm{i}\sin\theta(cosθ+isinθ)−1=cosθ−isinθ.]
hints: You may assume the positive-integer case, so the task is to reduce a negative power to a positive one.
Since ∣cos⁡θ+isin⁡θ∣=1|\cos\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin\theta|=1∣cosθ+isinθ∣=1, its reciprocal equals its conjugate — and that conjugate is the same expression evaluated at angle −θ-\theta−θ.
So (cos⁡θ+isin⁡θ)−m(\cos\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin\theta)^{-m}(cosθ+isinθ)−m becomes the positive-integer case applied at angle −θ-\theta−θ. Do not forget to dispose of n=0n=0n=0 as well.
problems.format: (cos θ + i sin θ)⁻³ at θ = π/6

problems.html: Find all: (a) square roots of 2i2\mathrm{i}2i; (b) cube roots of −1-1−1; (c) fourth roots of −1-1−1; (d) fifth roots of 323232 (leave in exponential form).
hints: The same procedure in every part: exponential form, then modulus ρ=r1/n\rho=r^{1/n}ρ=r1/n and arguments (θ+2πk)/n(\theta+2\pi k)/n(θ+2πk)/n.
Expect exactly nnn roots, equally spaced by 2πn\tfrac{2\pi}{n}n2π​ on a circle of radius ρ\rhoρ — a quick check that none has been lost.
In (b) and (c) the number is −1=eiπ-1=\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\pi}−1=eiπ, so the first argument is π/n\pi/nπ/n rather than 000, which rotates the whole polygon off the real axis.
problems.format: square roots of 2i; positive real part first

problems.html: The argument of 5−12i5-12\mathrm{i}5−12i is not a standard angle, so the exponential method is awkward. Instead find both square roots of 5−12i5-12\mathrm{i}5−12i in Cartesian form by equating real and imaginary parts of (a+ib)2(a+\mathrm{i}b)^{2}(a+ib)2, and verify by squaring.
hints: Set (a+ib)2=5−12i(a+\mathrm{i}b)^{2}=5-12\mathrm{i}(a+ib)2=5−12i, expand the left side, and match real and imaginary parts.
That gives a2−b2=5a^{2}-b^{2}=5a2−b2=5 and 2ab=−122ab=-122ab=−12. A third equation comes free from the moduli: a2+b2=∣5−12i∣a^{2}+b^{2}=|5-12\mathrm{i}|a2+b2=∣5−12i∣.
Adding and subtracting the two equations in a2a^{2}a2 and b2b^{2}b2 isolates each. Then let the sign of 2ab2ab2ab decide whether aaa and bbb share a sign or not.
problems.format: both square roots; positive real part first

problems.html: Solve z3=1+iz^{3}=1+\mathrm{i}z3=1+i, leaving the roots in exponential form.
hints: Nothing changes because the right-hand side is not real. Convert it to exponential form and apply the same root formula as before.
1+i=21/2eiπ/41+\mathrm{i}=2^{1/2}\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\pi/4}1+i=21/2eiπ/4, so each root has modulus (21/2)1/3=21/6\left(2^{1/2}\right)^{1/3}=2^{1/6}(21/2)1/3=21/6.
The arguments are π/4+2πk3\dfrac{\pi/4+2\pi k}{3}3π/4+2πk​ for k=0,1,2k=0,1,2k=0,1,2. Leave them in that form: these angles are not standard, so a Cartesian conversion would only obscure the answer.
problems.format: the arguments for k = 0, 1, 2; π as pi

problems.html: Solve z6=64z^{6}=64z6=64, giving all six roots in Cartesian form, and describe their configuration.
hints: 646464 is real and positive, so it is 64 ei064\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}0}64ei0 and the arguments start from zero.
Each root has modulus 641/6=264^{1/6}=2641/6=2, and the arguments are 2πk6=πk3\tfrac{2\pi k}{6}=\tfrac{\pi k}{3}62πk​=3πk​.
So the roots are exactly twice the sixth roots of unity: six points a sixth of a turn apart on the circle of radius 222. Two of them land on the real axis.
problems.format: the two real roots, comma-separated

problems.html: In an NNN-point discrete Fourier transform the sampling frequencies are the NNNth roots of unity. Take N=4N=4N=4 and ω=ei2π/4\omega=\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}2\pi/4}ω=ei2π/4. (a) List ω0,ω1,ω2,ω3\omega^{0},\omega^{1},\omega^{2},\omega^{3}ω0,ω1,ω2,ω3. (b) Show that ∑k=03ωk=0\sum_{k=0}^{3}\omega^{k}=0∑k=03​ωk=0 and ∑k=03ω2k=0\sum_{k=0}^{3}\omega^{2k}=0∑k=03​ω2k=0, whereas ∑k=03ω0⋅k=4\sum_{k=0}^{3}\omega^{0\cdot k}=4∑k=03​ω0⋅k=4. [These “orthogonality” sums are what make the DFT invertible.]
hints: With N=4N=4N=4 the number ω=ei2π/4=eiπ/2\omega=\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}2\pi/4}=\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\pi/2}ω=ei2π/4=eiπ/2 is one you already know well.
For the sums, note that ω2=−1\omega^{2}=-1ω2=−1, so the second sum simply alternates 1,−1,1,−11,-1,1,-11,−1,1,−1.
In the third sum every term is ω0=1\omega^{0}=1ω0=1, which is why it comes out as NNN rather than 000. That contrast between the two cases is the whole orthogonality relation.
problems.format: the three sums in (b), comma-separated

problems.html: The fast Fourier transform is built from the “twiddle factors” WNk=e−i2πk/NW_{N}^{k}=\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}2\pi k/N}WNk​=e−i2πk/N. Take N=8N=8N=8. (a) Write W81W_{8}^{1}W81​ in Cartesian form. (b) Show that W8k+4=− W8kW_{8}^{k+4}=-\,W_{8}^{k}W8k+4​=−W8k​ for every integer kkk (the symmetry that halves the FFT’s work). (c) Give the modulus and argument of W83W_{8}^{3}W83​.
hints: Every twiddle factor is e\mathrm{e}e raised to a purely imaginary power, so all of them lie on the unit circle.

For (b), split the exponent: e−i2π(k+4)/8=e−i2πk/8⋅e−iπ\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}2\pi(k+4)/8}=\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}2\pi k/8}\cdot\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}\pi}e−i2π(k+4)/8=e−i2πk/8⋅e−iπ, then evaluate the second factor.
For (c) the modulus needs no computation at all, and the argument is just −2πkN-\tfrac{2\pi k}{N}−N2πk​ with k=3k=3k=3 and N=8N=8N=8.
problems.format: modulus and argument of W₈³; π as pi

problems.html: (a) Verify that z=2iz=2\mathrm{i}z=2i is a root of z2+4z^{2}+4z2+4, and write down the other. (b) Factor z4+4z^{4}+4z4+4 into two real quadratics. [Hint: find the four roots first.]
hints: For (a) substitute and check; the conjugate-pair property then hands you the other root with no work.
For (b) solve z4=−4z^{4}=-4z4=−4 with the root formula — the four roots come out as ±1±i\pm1\pm\mathrm{i}±1±i.

To get real quadratic factors, pair each root with its conjugate: (z−(1+i))(z−(1−i))\bigl(z-(1+\mathrm{i})\bigr)\bigl(z-(1-\mathrm{i})\bigr)(z−(1+i))(z−(1−i)) multiplies out with no i\mathrm{i}i surviving.
problems.format: the other root of z²+4

problems.html: Let ω=ei2π/5\omega=\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}2\pi/5}ω=ei2π/5. Show that (1−ω)(1−ω2)(1−ω3)(1−ω4)=5(1-\omega)(1-\omega^{2})(1-\omega^{3})(1-\omega^{4})=5(1−ω)(1−ω2)(1−ω3)(1−ω4)=5. Generalise to nnn.
hints: Start from the complete factorisation zn−1=∏k=0n−1(z−ωk)z^{n}-1=\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}(z-\omega^{k})zn−1=∏k=0n−1​(z−ωk), which the fundamental theorem guarantees.
Divide both sides by z−1z-1z−1 to remove the k=0k=0k=0 factor; the left-hand side becomes 1+z+⋯+zn−11+z+\dots+z^{n-1}1+z+⋯+zn−1.
Now substitute z=1z=1z=1 into that identity and simply count the terms on the left-hand side.
problems.format: the value of the product

problems.html: Find all z∈Cz\in\mathbb{C}z∈C with z2=z‾z^{2}=\overline{z}z2=z.
hints: Polar form is far easier here than Cartesian: write z=r eiθz=r\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}z=reiθ and note that zˉ=r e−iθ\bar z=r\,\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}\theta}zˉ=re−iθ.
Matching moduli gives r2=rr^{2}=rr2=r. Deal with the case r=0r=0r=0 separately, before you divide by rrr.

Matching arguments gives 2θ≡−θ2\theta\equiv-\theta2θ≡−θ modulo 2π2\pi2π, so 3θ3\theta3θ is a whole number of turns. Count the distinct θ\thetaθ that allows, and do not lose the solution you set aside.
problems.format: how many solutions there are

problems.html: Use De Moivre to show cos⁡4θ=8cos⁡4θ−8cos⁡2θ+1\cos 4\theta=8\cos^{4}\theta-8\cos^{2}\theta+1cos4θ=8cos4θ−8cos2θ+1.
hints: Take the real part of (cos⁡θ+isin⁡θ)4(\cos\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin\theta)^{4}(cosθ+isinθ)4, which by De Moivre is cos⁡4θ\cos4\thetacos4θ.

In the binomial expansion the real terms are those carrying an even power of i\mathrm{i}i: cos⁡4θ−6cos⁡2θsin⁡2θ+sin⁡4θ\cos^{4}\theta-6\cos^{2}\theta\sin^{2}\theta+\sin^{4}\thetacos4θ−6cos2θsin2θ+sin4θ.

Now eliminate the sines with sin⁡2θ=1−cos⁡2θ\sin^{2}\theta=1-\cos^{2}\thetasin2θ=1−cos2θ and expand carefully — the (1−cos⁡2θ)2(1-\cos^{2}\theta)^{2}(1−cos2θ)2 term is where the errors usually happen.
problems.format: the three coefficients in cos 4θ

problems.html: Use the inverse Euler formula to express cos⁡5θ\cos^{5}\thetacos5θ as a sum of cosines of multiples of θ\thetaθ.
hints: Use cos⁡θ=12(eiθ+e−iθ)\cos\theta=\tfrac12\left(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}+\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}\theta}\right)cosθ=21​(eiθ+e−iθ) and expand the fifth power binomially.
The factor in front is 125=132\tfrac{1}{2^{5}}=\tfrac{1}{32}251​=321​, and the binomial coefficients are 1,5,10,10,5,11,5,10,10,5,11,5,10,10,5,1.
Pair the outermost terms into 2cos⁡5θ2\cos5\theta2cos5θ, the next pair into 2cos⁡3θ2\cos3\theta2cos3θ and the middle pair into 2cos⁡θ2\cos\theta2cosθ; every exponential then disappears.
problems.format: the cos5θ, cos3θ and cosθ coefficients

problems.html: Show that tan⁡3θ=3tan⁡θ−tan⁡3θ1−3tan⁡2θ\displaystyle\tan 3\theta=\frac{3\tan\theta-\tan^{3}\theta}{1-3\tan^{2}\theta}tan3θ=1−3tan2θ3tanθ−tan3θ​.
hints: Do not start from scratch — divide the sin⁡3θ\sin3\thetasin3θ identity by the cos⁡3θ\cos3\thetacos3θ identity you already have.
Then divide the numerator and the denominator by cos⁡3θ\cos^{3}\thetacos3θ, so that every term turns into a power of tan⁡θ\tan\thetatanθ.
You will need 1cos⁡2θ=1+tan⁡2θ\dfrac{1}{\cos^{2}\theta}=1+\tan^{2}\thetacos2θ1​=1+tan2θ to convert the leftover factors; apply it on both the top and the bottom.
problems.format: the value of tan 3θ when θ = π/12

problems.html: Using the geometric series for ∑k=0n−1eikθ\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}k\theta}∑k=0n−1​eikθ (with θ≠0 mod 2π\theta\ne 0\bmod 2\piθ=0mod2π), show that ∑k=0n−1cos⁡kθ=sin⁡(nθ/2)sin⁡(θ/2) cos⁡ ⁣((n−1)θ2).\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\cos k\theta=\frac{\sin(n\theta/2)}{\sin(\theta/2)}\, \cos\!\Bigl(\tfrac{(n-1)\theta}{2}\Bigr).k=0∑n−1​coskθ=sin(θ/2)sin(nθ/2)​cos(2(n−1)θ​).
hints: The cosine sum is the real part of ∑k=0n−1eikθ\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}k\theta}∑k=0n−1​eikθ, which is an ordinary geometric series with ratio eiθ\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}eiθ.
Sum it to einθ−1eiθ−1\dfrac{\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}n\theta}-1}{\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}-1}eiθ−1einθ−1​, then factor a half-angle exponential out of the numerator and out of the denominator.

Each bracket then has the shape eiϕ−e−iϕ=2isin⁡ϕ\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\phi}-\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}\phi}=2\mathrm{i}\sin\phieiϕ−e−iϕ=2isinϕ. The two factors of 2i2\mathrm{i}2i cancel, leaving one exponential times a ratio of sines.
problems.format: the sum when n = 4 and θ = π/2

problems.html: Show that cosh⁡(ix)=cos⁡x\cosh(\mathrm{i}x)=\cos xcosh(ix)=cosx and sinh⁡(ix)=isin⁡x\sinh(\mathrm{i}x)=\mathrm{i}\sin xsinh(ix)=isinx, and evaluate sin⁡(2i)\sin(2\mathrm{i})sin(2i) and cos⁡(πi)\cos(\pi\mathrm{i})cos(πi) in terms of e\mathrm{e}e.
hints: The same method as before: substitute a purely imaginary argument into the inverse Euler formulas.

cosh⁡(ix)=12(eix+e−ix)\cosh(\mathrm{i}x)=\tfrac12\left(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}x}+\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}x}\right)cosh(ix)=21​(eix+e−ix) is literally the formula for cos⁡x\cos xcosx; the sine case picks up a factor of i\mathrm{i}i along the way.

For the evaluations, run the earlier link in the other direction — sin⁡(ix)=isinh⁡x\sin(\mathrm{i}x)=\mathrm{i}\sinh xsin(ix)=isinhx and cos⁡(ix)=cosh⁡x\cos(\mathrm{i}x)=\cosh xcos(ix)=coshx — then write the hyperbolic function out in exponentials.
problems.format: the value of cos(iπ), to 3 d.p.

problems.html: Starting from cos⁡2θ=1−2sin⁡2θ\cos 2\theta=1-2\sin^{2}\thetacos2θ=1−2sin2θ, set θ=ix\theta=\mathrm{i}xθ=ix and use the link of the previous exercise to derive the hyperbolic identity cosh⁡2x=1+2sinh⁡2x\cosh 2x=1+2\sinh^{2}xcosh2x=1+2sinh2x.
hints: Substitute θ=ix\theta=\mathrm{i}xθ=ix into the given trigonometric identity and translate each side using the link.
cos⁡2θ\cos2\thetacos2θ becomes cos⁡(2ix)=cosh⁡2x\cos(2\mathrm{i}x)=\cosh 2xcos(2ix)=cosh2x; now do the same for sin⁡θ\sin\thetasinθ.

The sign flip appears when you square: sin⁡2(ix)=(isinh⁡x)2=−sinh⁡2x\sin^{2}(\mathrm{i}x)=(\mathrm{i}\sinh x)^{2}=-\sinh^{2}xsin2(ix)=(isinhx)2=−sinh2x. That one minus sign is the whole reason hyperbolic identities differ from trigonometric ones.
problems.format: cosh 2x at x = 1, to 3 d.p.

problems.html: Combine 5cos⁡ωt+12sin⁡ωt5\cos\omega t+12\sin\omega t5cosωt+12sinωt into Rcos⁡(ωt−α)R\cos(\omega t-\alpha)Rcos(ωt−α), giving RRR exactly and α\alphaα to three decimals.
hints: Write the sine as a cosine with a phase, take both phasors, and add them as complex numbers.
12sin⁡ωt=12cos⁡(ωt−π2)12\sin\omega t=12\cos(\omega t-\tfrac{\pi}{2})12sinωt=12cos(ωt−2π​), so its phasor is −12i-12\mathrm{i}−12i and the sum is 5−12i5-12\mathrm{i}5−12i.
RRR is the modulus of that sum — another familiar triangle — and α\alphaα is the size of its argument, which the form Rcos⁡(ωt−α)R\cos(\omega t-\alpha)Rcos(ωt−α) takes as a positive lag.
problems.format: R, then α to 3 d.p.

problems.html: Two alternating voltages of equal amplitude but different phase, V1=10cos⁡ωtV_{1}=10\cos\omega tV1​=10cosωt and V2=10cos⁡(ωt+2π3)V_{2}=10\cos(\omega t+\tfrac{2\pi}{3})V2​=10cos(ωt+32π​) (volts), are added. Find the amplitude and phase of V1+V2V_{1}+V_{2}V1​+V2​.
hints: Convert each voltage to a phasor and add them; ωt\omega tωt never needs to be touched.
10 ei2π/3=10(−12+32i)10\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}2\pi/3}=10\left(-\tfrac12+\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\mathrm{i}\right)10ei2π/3=10(−21​+23​​i), so the real parts partly cancel when the two are added.
Take the modulus and argument of the sum. Two equal amplitudes 2π3\tfrac{2\pi}{3}32π​ apart give a resultant of the same amplitude — worth noticing, rather than assuming it must double.
problems.format: the amplitude and the phase; π as pi

problems.html: Show that three equal phasors 120∘120^{\circ}120∘ apart sum to zero: 1+ei2π/3+ei4π/3=01+\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}2\pi/3}+\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}4\pi/3}=01+ei2π/3+ei4π/3=0. Interpret the result physically.
hints: These three numbers are the cube roots of unity, so this is the n=3n=3n=3 case of a fact proved earlier in the sheet.
Either sum the geometric series, or convert each to Cartesian form and add: the imaginary parts cancel as a pair and the real parts give 1−12−121-\tfrac12-\tfrac121−21​−21​.
Physically, the three line voltages sum to zero at every instant. Say what that implies for the current carried by the neutral conductor.
problems.format: the sum of the three phasors

problems.html: Decide and justify briefly: (a) ∣eiθ∣=1\left|\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}\right|=1​eiθ​=1 for every real θ\thetaθ. (b) eiθ=eiφ\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}=\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\varphi}eiθ=eiφ implies θ=φ\theta=\varphiθ=φ. (c) Every complex number has exactly three cube roots. (d) The nnnth roots of unity always include 111.
hints: Three of these are settled straight from a definition; only one really calls for a counterexample.
For (b), remember that an argument is fixed only up to a whole number of turns.
For (c), the number of nnnth roots is nnn — but check whether that is true of every complex number, including the one that behaves differently from all the rest.
problems.format: (a)–(d): true or false, comma-separated

problems.html: A student writes: “Since (cos⁡θ+isin⁡θ)1/2=cos⁡θ2+isin⁡θ2(\cos\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin\theta)^{1/2} =\cos\tfrac{\theta}{2}+\mathrm{i}\sin\tfrac{\theta}{2}(cosθ+isinθ)1/2=cos2θ​+isin2θ​ by De Moivre, the square root of eiθ\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}eiθ is eiθ/2\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta/2}eiθ/2.” What is wrong, and what is the correct statement?
hints: Two separate things are wrong: an appeal to a theorem outside its stated range, and an answer that is incomplete.
De Moivre as proved covers integer nnn; taking n=12n=\tfrac12n=21​ is not justified by it, even in the cases where the resulting value happens to be correct.

More seriously, the argument of eiθ\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}eiθ is fixed only up to 2π2\pi2π, so halving θ+2πk\theta+2\pi kθ+2πk gives different values at k=0k=0k=0 and k=1k=1k=1. Work both out and compare them.
problems.format: how many square roots a nonzero z has

questions.stem: A student writes: 'by De Moivre with n=12n=\tfrac12n=21​, the square root of eiθ\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}eiθ is eiθ/2\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta/2}eiθ/2.' What is wrong?
options: Nothing — De Moivre holds for every real nnn.
De Moivre is proved for integer nnn, and in any case a non-zero number has two square roots, not one.
The formula is wrong; the square root is 12eiθ\tfrac12\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}21​eiθ.
eiθ\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}eiθ has a square root only when θ\thetaθ is a multiple of 2π2\pi2π.
questions.hint: Two things are worth checking: the values of nnn the theorem was actually proved for, and how many square roots a non-zero complex number has.
questions.why: Two separate faults. The theorem as proved covers n∈Zn\in\mathbb{Z}n∈Z, so n=12n=\tfrac12n=21​ is outside its range — the step is unjustified even where the value happens to be right. More seriously it loses a root: the argument of eiθ\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}eiθ is fixed only up to 2π2\pi2π, so the square roots are ei(θ+2πk)/2\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}(\theta+2\pi k)/2}ei(θ+2πk)/2 for k=0,1k=0,1k=0,1, namely eiθ/2\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta/2}eiθ/2 and −eiθ/2-\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta/2}−eiθ/2. The student's value is one of the two.

questions.stem: Does eiθ=eiφ\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}=\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\varphi}eiθ=eiφ force θ=φ\theta=\varphiθ=φ, for real θ\thetaθ and φ\varphiφ?
options: Yes, provided both angles are real.
No: an argument is fixed only up to a whole turn, so θ\thetaθ and φ\varphiφ may differ by a multiple of 2π2\pi2π.
No, because eiθ\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}eiθ is not one-to-one on any interval at all.
Yes — the exponential function is one-to-one.
questions.hint: Try θ=0\theta=0θ=0 and φ=2π\varphi=2\piφ=2π.
questions.why: The simplest counterexample is ei0=ei2π=1\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}0}=\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}2\pi}=1ei0=ei2π=1. The real exponential really is one-to-one, which is why the failure catches people out; but θ↦eiθ\theta\mapsto\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}θ↦eiθ wraps the real line repeatedly around the unit circle. It is one-to-one on any half-open interval of length 2π2\pi2π — which is precisely why the principal argument is defined on (−π,π](-\pi,\pi](−π,π] — so the last option overstates the failure. This ambiguity is not a defect: it is the source of every extra nnnth root.

questions.stem: Where in the Argand plane do the five fifth roots of a non-zero complex number zzz lie?
options: At five different distances from the origin, one for each root.
At the vertices of a regular pentagon, but only when zzz is real and positive.
Spread along a straight line through the origin.
At the vertices of a regular pentagon on the circle of radius ∣z∣1/5|z|^{1/5}∣z∣1/5.
questions.hint: All nnn roots share one modulus, so they share one circle. What is left to tell them apart, and by how much do consecutive ones differ?
questions.why: Every root has the same modulus, the real fifth root of ∣z∣|z|∣z∣, so all five sit on one circle. Consecutive arguments differ by 2π5\tfrac{2\pi}{5}52π​, because each root is the previous one multiplied by ei2π/5\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}2\pi/5}ei2π/5 — a rotation. Equal spacing on a circle is exactly a regular polygon. A non-zero argument for zzz turns the whole pentagon to match, but cannot change its shape, so the restriction in the last option is unnecessary.

questions.stem: Combining 3cos⁡ωt+4sin⁡ωt3\cos\omega t+4\sin\omega t3cosωt+4sinωt into a single sinusoid Rcos⁡(ωt−α)R\cos(\omega t-\alpha)Rcos(ωt−α), what is the amplitude RRR?
options: 333, since the cosine term is the one in phase.
7\sqrt77​.
555, the modulus of the phasor sum 3−4i3-4\mathrm{i}3−4i.
777, the sum of the two amplitudes.
questions.hint: Write 4sin⁡ωt4\sin\omega t4sinωt as a cosine with a phase shift, then add the two *phasors* as complex numbers rather than adding the amplitudes.
questions.why: Amplitudes add only when the two terms are in phase, and these are a quarter-turn apart. Writing 4sin⁡ωt=4cos⁡ ⁣(ωt−π2)4\sin\omega t=4\cos\!\left(\omega t-\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right)4sinωt=4cos(ωt−2π​) gives phasors 333 and −4i-4\mathrm{i}−4i, whose sum is 3−4i3-4\mathrm{i}3−4i — the 333–444–555 triangle again, so R=5R=5R=5. The phase follows from the argument: α=arctan⁡43≈0.927\alpha=\arctan\tfrac43\approx0.927α=arctan34​≈0.927. Adding to 777 would be right only if the phase difference were zero, and 7\sqrt77​ corresponds to no step in the calculation at all.

questions.stem: How many cube roots does the number 000 have?
options: One, namely 000 itself.
Three, like every other complex number.
Infinitely many.
None.
questions.hint: Put r=0r=0r=0 into ρ=r1/n\rho=r^{1/n}ρ=r1/n, then count how many *distinct* numbers the root formula can produce.
questions.why: The root formula wk=ρ ei(θ+2πk)/nw_k=\rho\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}(\theta+2\pi k)/n}wk​=ρei(θ+2πk)/n needs a modulus ρ=r1/n\rho=r^{1/n}ρ=r1/n. When r=0r=0r=0 that is 000 for every kkk, so all three candidates collapse onto the same number and the distinct arguments become meaningless. Zero is the single exception to 'every complex number has exactly nnn nnnth roots', and it is what makes the corresponding true/false item on the exercise sheet false. The fundamental theorem is untouched: z3=0z^3=0z3=0 still has three roots counted with multiplicity, all of them 000.

questions.stem: Substituting θ=ix\theta=\mathrm{i}xθ=ix turns trigonometric identities into hyperbolic ones. What single fact explains why the two families differ by signs?
options: It is a coincidence with no underlying reason.
sin⁡(ix)=isinh⁡x\sin(\mathrm{i}x)=\mathrm{i}\sinh xsin(ix)=isinhx, so squaring a sine introduces a factor of −1-1−1.
The hyperbolic functions are not periodic.
Hyperbolic functions are defined on a hyperbola rather than a circle.
questions.hint: Substitute θ=ix\theta=\mathrm{i}xθ=ix into cos⁡\coscos and into sin⁡\sinsin separately, and see which of the two picks up a stray factor.
questions.why: Cosines transfer unchanged, since cos⁡(ix)=cosh⁡x\cos(\mathrm{i}x)=\cosh xcos(ix)=coshx with no stray factor. Sines do not: sin⁡(ix)=isinh⁡x\sin(\mathrm{i}x)=\mathrm{i}\sinh xsin(ix)=isinhx, so sin⁡2(ix)=(isinh⁡x)2=−sinh⁡2x\sin^{2}(\mathrm{i}x)=(\mathrm{i}\sinh x)^{2}=-\sinh^{2}xsin2(ix)=(isinhx)2=−sinh2x. Every sign difference between the two families traces back to that one squared i\mathrm{i}i — the pattern usually quoted as Osborn's rule. The first and third options are perfectly true statements about hyperbolic functions, but neither of them predicts which signs flip.
